input.strategy_title: Queue-aware GPU scheduling for distributed training workloads
input.strategy_markdown:
## Problem Statement

Large training jobs fail or waste capacity because pods are admitted piecemeal:
a 16-GPU job can hold 12 GPUs for hours waiting for the last 4, starving other
teams, and partially scheduled jobs die on timeout. Customers running mixed
fleets also report that jobs land on suboptimal GPU topologies (crossing NVLink
domains) with significant throughput loss. We need admission and placement that
treats a multi-node training job as one unit and uses GPU topology where it
matters.

## High-Level Requirements

| ID | Priority | Requirement |
|-------|----------|-------------|
| HLR-1 | P0 | Multi-node training jobs are admitted all-or-nothing: no partial GPU occupation while waiting for remaining pods. |
| HLR-2 | P0 | Per-project GPU quota is enforced at admission time across training job types (PyTorchJob, RayJob). |
| HLR-3 | P1 | Users can see queue position, quota consumption, and admission state for their pending jobs in the Dashboard. |
| HLR-4 | P1 | Higher-priority workloads can preempt lower-priority ones according to an admin-defined policy. |
| HLR-5 | P2 | Job placement can prefer GPU-topology-aligned nodes when the cluster exposes topology information. |

## Affected Components

- Distributed Workloads
- Training Operator
- Dashboard

## Out of Scope

- GPU sharing/fractioning (MIG, time-slicing policy management)
- Cross-cluster or multi-cluster queueing

## Open Questions

1. Do Kueue's current gang-admission semantics (waitForPodsReady) actually
   satisfy HLR-1 for PyTorchJob and RayJob at our target scale, or do we need
   scheduler-plugin work (e.g. coscheduling) beyond Kueue? The answer changes
   the shape of most implementation work.
2. Topology-aware placement (HLR-5) depends on node topology discovery that is
   only Tech Preview — is it mature enough to build on this release?
3. What preemption semantics do reference customers actually need — full
   eviction with requeue, or checkpoint-aware graceful preemption? We have
   conflicting field signals and no benchmark of checkpoint overhead.

# Kueue-native gang admission configuration for multi-node training jobs

## Description

This branch epic delivers all-or-nothing (gang) admission of multi-node
training jobs using the platform's existing queueing system, taken in the
outcome where the gang-admission validation concluded that Kueue's
waitForPodsReady semantics are sufficient at target scale. It configures and
hardens Kueue gang admission so that a multi-node job either gets all its pods
and GPUs at once or holds nothing — no partial GPU occupation while waiting for
remaining pods, and no partially scheduled jobs dying on timeout.

## Scope

- Configure all-or-nothing admission semantics for multi-node PyTorchJob and
  RayJob workloads in the queueing system, per the validation's findings.
- Ensure admission timeouts evict the entire partial allocation (all pods,
  all GPUs) and requeue the job, so stranded partial allocations cannot occur.
- Verify workload integration for both job types: job pods are held until the
  full gang can be admitted.
- Validate that training jobs run correctly under gang admission (the Training
  Operator component requires no code change; its jobs must keep working — this
  is a validation acceptance criterion, not an implementation surface).

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a multi-node job requiring N GPUs, when only M < N GPUs are available,
  then the job holds zero GPUs while pending (no partial occupation).
- Given enough GPUs become available, when the job is admitted, then all of
  its pods start together as one unit.
- Given a job's pods fail to become ready within the admission timeout, when
  the timeout fires, then the entire partial allocation is released and the job
  is requeued.
- Given PyTorchJob and RayJob workloads, when run under gang admission, then
  both job types complete correctly (Training Operator passive validation).
- Given mixed fleets with other teams' jobs queued, when a large job waits for
  its full gang, then it does not starve other queues beyond configured
  policy.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-1 (P0, multi-node training jobs are admitted all-or-nothing: no partial
  GPU occupation while waiting for remaining pods): fully covered by this epic
  in outcome A (Kueue-native admission sufficient).

# Provision coscheduling scheduler-plugin for gang scheduling

## Description

This branch epic provisions a coscheduling scheduler-plugin as new scheduling
infrastructure for the platform, taken in the outcome where the gang-admission
validation concluded that the queueing system's native waitForPodsReady
semantics are insufficient at target scale. The plugin is not currently shipped
in the platform, so this epic covers its packaging, deployment, and basic
validation as gang-scheduling infrastructure; the job-type integration that
builds on it is a separate epic within this branch.

## Scope

- Select and package the coscheduling scheduler-plugin for the platform
  (midstream fork under the platform's orgs, per the platform's midstream
  conventions).
- Deploy the plugin so it runs alongside the existing scheduler without
  disrupting default scheduling for non-gang workloads.
- Integrate its deployment with the platform's component management so it can
  be enabled/configured as part of the distributed workloads stack.
- Validate gang-scheduling capability at the infrastructure level: pod groups
  are scheduled all-or-nothing in controlled tests.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The coscheduling scheduler-plugin is packaged and deployable as part of the
  platform's distributed workloads stack.
- Given the plugin is deployed, when a pod group is scheduled, then the group
  is placed all-or-nothing in validation tests (zero partial placement).
- Given the plugin is deployed, when ordinary (non-gang) workloads are
  scheduled, then default scheduling behavior is unchanged.
- The plugin's deployment can be enabled, disabled, and configured through
  supported platform configuration.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-1 (P0, multi-node training jobs are admitted all-or-nothing): this epic
  provides the gang-scheduling infrastructure that enables HLR-1 in outcome B
  (scheduler-plugin required); the job-type admission integration that
  completes HLR-1 is carried by the follow-on epic in this branch.

# AI Signal Rationale — RHAISTRAT-9005-BRANCH-B-E009 (Implementation, branch B)

| Signal | Value | Rationale |

| change_specificity | 0 | Job types and required behavior (all-or-nothing, quota preserved, timeout release) are enumerated, but the pod-group integration surface per job type is undesigned until the plugin is provisioned. |
| pattern_precedent | 1 | Both PyTorchJob and RayJob already integrate with the queueing system for admission; extending those integrations to a new gang mechanism follows existing patterns. |
| adapter_pattern | 0 | Integration work, but no single reference implementation covers plugin-based gang semantics for both job types. |

| external_dependency | -1 | Depends on the external upstream scheduler-plugin project's semantics and release, and possibly on upstream job-operator behavior for pod-group markings. |
| human_process_gates | 0 | No approval step beyond normal review; the security review attaches to the plugin provisioning, not this integration. |
| repo_access | 1 | Training-operator, kuberay, and plugin midstream repos are accessible. |
| architecture_claims | 0 | The job-type integration surface is documented in architecture context, but the plugin-based gang path itself is outside the platform inventory, so claims are only partially substantiated. |

# Gang admission integration for training jobs via scheduler plugin

## Description

This branch epic integrates multi-node training workloads (PyTorchJob and
RayJob) with the coscheduling scheduler-plugin provisioned earlier in this
branch, so that training jobs are admitted all-or-nothing: a job either gets
its full pod set and GPUs at once or holds nothing. It is the outcome-B
counterpart of the queueing-system configuration work, taken when the
gang-admission validation concluded that scheduler-plugin support is required.

## Scope

- Integrate PyTorchJob workloads with the scheduler plugin's pod-group
  semantics so job pods are scheduled as one gang (may require
  training-operator-side changes to emit the required pod-group markings).
- Integrate RayJob workloads with the same gang semantics.
- Keep per-project GPU quota enforced at admission with the plugin active
  (quota accounting must survive the change of admission mechanism).
- Validate end-to-end behavior for both job types, including admission
  timeouts releasing the entire partial allocation.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a PyTorchJob requiring N GPUs, when only M < N GPUs are available,
  then the job holds zero GPUs while pending.
- Given a RayJob with a multi-node actor/worker topology, when its full gang
  cannot be admitted, then no partial allocation is held.
- Given the scheduler plugin is active, when jobs are admitted, then
  per-project GPU quota is still enforced at admission time.
- Given a job's pods fail to become ready within the admission timeout, when
  the timeout fires, then the entire partial allocation is released and the
  job is requeued.
- Given both job types running under plugin-based gang admission, when jobs
  complete, then training results are correct (Training Operator validation;
  operator-side changes, if any, are included in this scope).

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-1 (P0, multi-node training jobs are admitted all-or-nothing: no partial
  GPU occupation while waiting for remaining pods): completes HLR-1 coverage in
  outcome B, building on the scheduler-plugin provisioning epic in this branch.

## Risks / Notes

- Sequencing note: the per-project GPU quota preservation criterion above is a
  cross-feature check against the per-project GPU quota enforcement at
  admission, a parallel main-plan deliverable. Validate it after that quota
  enforcement work has landed so a failure localizes correctly (quota
  accounting versus plugin-based admission). Plugin provisioning, job-type
  integration, and gang-admission construction do not consume that
  deliverable's output, so no build dependency is introduced — this is a
  validation-ordering constraint only.

# Validate Kueue all-or-nothing admission for multi-node training jobs

## Description

This investigation resolves whether the platform's queueing system (Kueue, using
its waitForPodsReady gang-admission semantics) satisfies the all-or-nothing
admission requirement for multi-node PyTorchJob and RayJob workloads at the
target scale, or whether additional scheduler-plugin work (e.g. a coscheduling
plugin) is required. The strategy flags this as the open question that "changes
the shape of most implementation work": the answer selects between a
Kueue-native configuration path and a scheduler-plugin provisioning path for
gang admission. The deliverable is a decision document with benchmark evidence
and a recommendation that downstream implementation planning builds on.

## Scope

- Quantify the target scale the validation must cover (training job sizes in
  GPUs/pods, queue depth, cluster size, mix of PyTorchJob and RayJob), since the
  strategy references "our target scale" without defining it.
- Exercise Kueue's waitForPodsReady admission for multi-node PyTorchJob and
  RayJob workloads at that scale: verify that pods are admitted all-or-nothing
  and that no partial GPU occupation persists while a job waits for its
  remaining pods.
- Characterize failure modes: behavior when pods fail to become ready,
  admission timeouts, node loss mid-admission, and whether partially scheduled
  jobs release all held GPUs.
- Assess the coscheduling scheduler-plugin alternative (upstream maturity,
  operational cost of running a custom scheduler plugin on the platform,
  compatibility with the existing Kueue quota model).
- Produce a recommendation with two bounded outcomes: (A) Kueue-native
  admission is sufficient, or (B) scheduler-plugin work is required — each with
  an estimate of downstream implementation scope.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A documented, agreed target-scale definition (job sizes, concurrency, queue
  depth, cluster capacity) is included in the decision document.
- For each job type (PyTorchJob, RayJob), benchmark evidence records a
  pass/fail result for all-or-nothing admission at target scale: either zero
  partial GPU occupation while pending, or a documented counterexample.
- Failure-mode behavior of waitForPodsReady (pods not ready, timeouts,
  mid-admission node loss) is documented with observed GPU release behavior.
- A written recommendation selects outcome A or outcome B, with rationale and
  downstream scope implications for each rejected alternative.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-1 (P0, all-or-nothing admission of multi-node training jobs): this
  investigation gates the implementation work that delivers HLR-1; it resolves
  which implementation approach (Kueue-native vs scheduler-plugin) is used.

# Determine required preemption semantics and checkpoint overhead

## Description

This investigation resolves which preemption semantics higher-priority workloads
actually need: full eviction with requeue, or checkpoint-aware graceful
preemption. The strategy records conflicting field signals and no benchmark of
checkpoint overhead, and the answer determines the scope of the preemption
implementation (Kueue preemption configuration alone, versus checkpoint
integration with the training stack). The deliverable is a requirements summary
from the field plus a checkpoint-overhead benchmark and a semantics
recommendation.

## Scope

- Collect and reconcile the conflicting field/customer signals on required
  preemption semantics for distributed training workloads.
- Benchmark checkpoint save and restore overhead for representative multi-node
  training jobs (time, storage, and job-progress loss), since no such benchmark
  exists today.
- Characterize what full eviction with requeue costs users of long-running
  training jobs (lost progress since last checkpoint or job start).
- Produce a recommendation: full eviction with requeue vs checkpoint-aware
  graceful preemption, including what an admin-defined preemption policy must
  be able to express in either case.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Field requirements are documented: which reference customers need which
  semantics, with the conflicting signals reconciled or explicitly escalated.
- A checkpoint-overhead benchmark for representative multi-node training jobs
  is produced, with measured save/restore times and storage footprint.
- A written recommendation selects the preemption semantics and states the
  policy surface admins need, so the preemption implementation can be scoped
  without further discovery.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-4 (P1, higher-priority workloads preempt lower-priority ones per
  admin-defined policy): this investigation gates the preemption
  implementation; its outcome determines whether that work is queue-configuration
  only or also requires checkpoint integration.

# Assess topology-aware scheduling Tech Preview maturity

## Description

This investigation determines whether node topology discovery — currently Tech
Preview in the platform's distributed workloads stack — is mature enough to
build GPU-topology-aware placement on in this release. The strategy makes
topology-aligned placement (HLR-5) conditional on this maturity. The deliverable
is a go/no-go assessment with evidence, so the placement work either proceeds
with a known-solid foundation or is deferred rather than built on shifting
ground.

## Scope

- Inventory the documented limitations of Tech Preview topology-aware
  scheduling from upstream release notes, issue trackers, and known gaps.
- Exercise node topology discovery on representative GPU nodes (e.g. NVLink
  domain reporting) and verify the reported topology is accurate and stable.
- Evaluate how the scheduler consumes topology information for placement
  decisions and whether the integration surface is stable enough to depend on.
- Produce a go/no-go recommendation for building topology-aligned placement in
  this release, with a fallback (defer to a later release) if maturity is
  insufficient.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A documented list of Tech Preview limitations with their impact on
  topology-aware placement, each sourced from upstream documentation or issues.
- Evidence from representative GPU nodes that discovered topology (e.g. NVLink
  domains) matches the actual hardware topology, or a documented discrepancy.
- A written go/no-go recommendation for this release, with explicit criteria
  and the deferral fallback described.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-5 (P2, placement can prefer GPU-topology-aligned nodes when the cluster
  exposes topology information): this investigation gates whether the placement
  implementation ships in this release at all.

# Enforce per-project GPU quota at admission time

## Description

This epic enforces per-project GPU quota at admission time across training job
types (PyTorchJob and RayJob), using the queueing system's existing quota model
(ClusterQueue/LocalQueue). Jobs whose aggregate GPU request exceeds the
project's quota remain pending at admission — they do not occupy GPUs — so
over-subscription by one project cannot starve others. This delivers HLR-2 and
is independent of which gang-admission mechanism is ultimately selected, because
quota accounting happens at admission in either case.

## Scope

- Design the mapping of per-project GPU quota onto the queueing system's quota
  primitives (ClusterQueue/LocalQueue structure, cohorts, borrowing rules).
- Ensure quota is accounted at admission time for both PyTorchJob and RayJob
  workloads, with GPU requests aggregated per project across job types.
- Ensure jobs that exceed quota stay pending without holding any GPUs.
- Provide admin-facing configuration for per-project GPU quota limits.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a project with GPU quota X, when training jobs (PyTorchJob and RayJob)
  whose aggregate GPU request exceeds X are submitted, then the excess jobs
  remain pending and occupy zero GPUs.
- Given available quota within a project, when a job fitting the remaining
  quota is submitted, then it is admitted.
- Given jobs of both types from the same project, when quota consumption is
  measured, then it is attributable to the project as a single aggregate.
- Given an admin changes a project's GPU quota, when subsequent jobs are
  admitted, then the new limit is enforced without requiring job resubmission.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-2 (P0, per-project GPU quota enforced at admission time across training
  job types): fully covered by this epic.

# Admin-defined preemption policy for higher-priority workloads

## Description

This epic implements workload preemption according to an admin-defined policy:
when a higher-priority workload needs resources held by a lower-priority one,
the lower-priority workload is preempted per the policy and requeued. The
preemption semantics (full eviction with requeue versus checkpoint-aware
graceful preemption) are determined by the preemption-semantics investigation
this epic is gated on; the scope below covers both possibilities, with the
checkpoint integration included only if that outcome is selected.

## Scope

- Configure workload priorities and the admin-defined preemption policy in the
  queueing system (which priority levels may preempt which, and requeue
  behavior of preempted workloads).
- Ensure preempted workloads are requeued and later re-admitted when resources
  free up, without operator intervention.
- If checkpoint-aware graceful preemption is the selected semantics: integrate
  checkpoint save on eviction and restore on re-admission for training jobs,
  using the checkpoint-overhead benchmark to set sensible defaults.
- Validate that preemption interacts correctly with per-project GPU quota
  (preempted resources return to the project's quota pool).

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given an admin-defined preemption policy, when a higher-priority workload
  requires resources held by a lower-priority workload, then the lower-priority
  workload is preempted according to the policy.
- Given a preempted workload, when resources become available, then it is
  requeued and re-admitted automatically.
- Given preemption occurs, when quota is recomputed, then the preempted
  workload's GPU allocation is released back to its project's quota.
- Given checkpoint-aware semantics are selected, when a workload is gracefully
  preempted, then it resumes from its last checkpoint rather than restarting
  (or restarts, if full-eviction semantics are selected — per the gating
  investigation's outcome).
- Preemption is configurable by admins (policy on/off, which priorities
  preempt which) via supported configuration.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-4 (P1, higher-priority workloads can preempt lower-priority ones
  according to an admin-defined policy): fully covered by this epic.

## Risks / Notes

- Sequencing note: the quota-release acceptance criterion above verifies
  behavior that depends on the per-project GPU quota enforcement at admission
  (a separate, parallel deliverable in this plan). Validate that criterion
  only after the per-project GPU quota enforcement work has landed, so a
  failure localizes to preemption rather than to quota accounting. The
  preemption construction itself does not consume that deliverable's output,
  so no build dependency is introduced — this is a validation-ordering
  constraint only.

# Topology-aware GPU placement preference

## Description

This epic makes job placement prefer GPU-topology-aligned nodes when the
cluster exposes topology information, addressing the throughput loss reported
when training jobs land on pods crossing NVLink domains. It is gated on the
topology-maturity assessment: it only proceeds in this release if node topology
discovery (currently Tech Preview) is judged mature enough to build on; if not,
this epic is removed from the release plan and deferred.

## Scope

- Consume node topology information (e.g. NVLink domains) exposed by the
  cluster's topology discovery, per the maturity assessment's findings.
- Implement placement preference so that a training job's GPU allocation is
  topology-aligned where possible (pods placed within aligned topology domains).
- Ensure graceful fallback: when the cluster does not expose topology
  information, placement falls back to default scheduling behavior with no
  degradation.
- Keep the behavior a preference, not a hard requirement — jobs must still be
  schedulable when perfectly aligned placement is impossible.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a cluster exposing topology information, when a multi-node training job
  is placed, then its pods are placed on topology-aligned nodes according to
  the preference policy.
- Given a cluster that does not expose topology information, when a job is
  scheduled, then placement falls back to default behavior and the job still
  runs.
- Given aligned placement is impossible (fragmented topology), when a job is
  scheduled, then it is still admitted rather than blocked.
- Given topology-aligned versus non-aligned placements of a representative
  job, when throughput is compared, then the aligned placement shows the
  expected improvement (validating the feature does what it exists for).

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-5 (P2, job placement can prefer GPU-topology-aligned nodes when the
  cluster exposes topology information): fully covered by this epic.

# Dashboard visibility into queue position, quota, and admission state

## Description

This epic gives users visibility into their pending distributed training jobs
in the Dashboard: queue position, per-project GPU quota consumption, and
admission state. Users currently cannot see why a job is pending or how much
quota it consumes; this epic surfaces the queueing state that the platform's
admission and quota enforcement produce. It builds on the per-project quota
model (the quota structures whose consumption it displays) and reads workload
admission state and queue metrics exposed by the queueing system.

## Scope

- Add Dashboard surface (view/section) listing pending distributed workloads
  with their queue position, admission state (pending/admitted), and per-project
  GPU quota consumption.
- Read queue and workload state from the queueing system's Kubernetes CRs
  (Workload) and its exposed queue metrics; the Dashboard owns no data plane.
- Gate the new surface behind the Dashboard's existing per-component feature
  flag mechanism (OdhDashboardConfig).
- Keep existing distributed workload status views unaffected.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a pending training job, when the user opens the Dashboard, then the
  job's queue position, admission state, and its project's quota consumption
  are displayed.
- Given a job transitions from pending to admitted, when the Dashboard view is
  refreshed, then the admission state shown matches the queueing system's
  actual state.
- Given the feature flag is disabled, when the Dashboard is loaded, then the
  new surface is hidden and existing views are unchanged.
- Given workloads from multiple projects, when a user views quota consumption,
  then only their project's consumption is shown (project-scoped RBAC
  respected).

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-3 (P1, users can see queue position, quota consumption, and admission
  state for their pending jobs in the Dashboard): fully covered by this epic.
